definition.text: An artificial wetland built to clean sewage, greywater, stormwater runoff or industrial wastewater.

facts.text: It is an engineered system that uses the natural work of plants, soil and microorganisms to give wastewater a secondary treatment.
Plant roots, stems and leaves give microorganisms a surface to grow on while they break down organic material.
Physical, chemical and biological processes act together in the wetland to remove contaminants such as nitrogen, phosphorus and dissolved metals.
Constructed wetlands copy natural wetlands to capture stormwater, cut nutrient loads and create varied wildlife habitat.
Because they largely run themselves, their lifetime costs are much lower than those of conventional treatment plants, and their building costs are often lower too.
They need a lot of space, so they are not favoured where land is expensive.
Cattails and common reed are the main plants used, even though both can become invasive outside their native range.
Stormwater wetlands can act as 'ecological traps' for amphibians, whose larvae suffer from the pollutants that collect there.

definition.text: A constructed wetland in which the wastewater flows among plant roots below a gravel surface, so no water shows at the top.

facts.text: Keeping water below the surface makes the system more efficient, less smelly, less attractive to mosquitoes and less affected by winter.
It needs less land to treat water than a surface flow wetland.
Its cost depends mainly on the sand used to fill the bed.
It is a secondary treatment, so solids must first be removed by a primary treatment step.

definition.text: A constructed wetland with open water flowing horizontally across plant roots, also called a free water surface wetland.

facts.text: It is used to polish effluent from wastewater treatment plants and to treat stormwater drainage.
Sunlight, predators, settling and natural decay destroy pathogens in the open water.
It needs more land than a subsurface system and may smell more and work less well in winter.
Open water can breed mosquitoes, which makes it harder to fit into city neighbourhoods.

title: Green infrastructure

definition.text: A network of natural or nature-like features, also called blue-green infrastructure, used to solve urban and climate problems by building with nature.

facts.text: When people harness nature and use it as an infrastructure system, it is called green infrastructure.
Nature can protect communities from flooding or extreme heat and improve air, soil and water quality.
Its main parts include stormwater management, climate adaptation, reducing heat stress, biodiversity, food production, cleaner air and water, and recreation and shade.
The term has no widely agreed definition and is often expanded to 'multifunctional' green infrastructure, meaning several functions share the same land.
Its stormwater ideas began in mid-1980s proposals for practices to reduce runoff volume and erosion and recharge aquifers.
The term itself first appeared in the early 1990s, in a 1994 report on the Florida Greenways Project.
Examples include urban forests, constructed wetlands, green roofs, rain gardens, stormwater basins and bioswales.

distinct_from: Economics of green versus grey infrastructure

title: Blue infrastructure

definition.text: City infrastructure that involves water, such as rivers, ponds, lakes and harbours.

facts.text: When combined with green infrastructure it is called blue-green infrastructure.
It can support aquatic insects, amphibians and water birds in cities.
Accessible blue infrastructure is also called blue space, and access to it may benefit people's health and wellbeing.

distinct_from: Economics of green versus grey infrastructure

title: Green and blue roofs

definition.text: Roofs covered with plants and soil (green roofs) or built to collect and hold rainfall (blue roofs).

facts.text: Green roofs improve air and water quality and lower energy costs.
Green roofs can hold back forty to eighty percent of the rain that falls on them and release the rest slowly.
Blue roofs store rainfall and drain it to sewers and waterways at a controlled rate.
Zurich has required since 1991 that flat roofs not used as terraces be greened.

distinct_from: Economics of green versus grey infrastructure

title: Constructed floating wetland

definition.text: A planted structure that floats on a lake, river, estuary or coastal water and supports wetland vegetation.

facts.text: Its plants can remove heavy metals and nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen, and may store carbon.
It gives habitat to insects and wildlife and makes hardened urban shorelines look better.

distinct_from: Economics of green versus grey infrastructure

title: Downspout disconnection

definition.text: Cutting a roof's downspout off from the sewer and sending the roof water onto ground that can soak it up.

facts.text: In heavy rain a building's downspouts can send 12 gallons of water a minute into the sewer, raising the risk of basement backups and overflows.
It is especially useful in cities with combined sewer systems.

distinct_from: Economics of green versus grey infrastructure

title: Stormwater basin

definition.text: A planted hollow in the ground that collects rainwater to cut runoff to sewers, reduce erosion, filter water and prevent flooding.

facts.text: Newer designs with sturdier plants instead of mowed grass, often called bioretention basins, are good at removing pollutants and trapping sediment.
Stormwater basins are an important part of the sponge city idea for managing floods.

distinct_from: Economics of green versus grey infrastructure

title: Economics of green versus grey infrastructure

definition.text: The comparison of costs and benefits between green infrastructure and conventional 'grey' infrastructure such as concrete pipes and tunnels.

facts.text: A 2012 study of 479 US green infrastructure projects found 44% reduced costs while 31% increased them.
The largest savings came from less stormwater runoff and lower heating and cooling bills.
Philadelphia found a green plan would cost $1.2 billion over 25 years, against $6 billion for a grey plan.
Philadelphia's plan was also expected to raise property values by $390 million over 45 years, increasing the city's property tax income.
New York City's green plan was expected to cost $1.5 billion less than a comparable grey approach.
A 2016 UK study found residents were willing to pay more for green infrastructure that was visibly greener, accessible and multifunctional.
In fragile states, upfront building costs for green infrastructure were up to 8% higher than for other projects.

title: Green gentrification

definition.text: The displacement of lower-income residents when new green spaces raise property values and attract wealthier people.

facts.text: Projects meant to make cities greener and more liveable, as in Chicago, often raise social justice concerns such as gentrification.
Their benefits are often unevenly shared, usually serving wealthier, whiter neighbourhoods.
A study of Los Angeles housing prices linked green infrastructure to 'green climate gentrification'.
Greening can push out homeless people and others with poor access to housing, undoing some of its benefits.
Planners are urged to combine environmental goals with social equity and to work with community residents.
Green amenities include green spaces, parks, green roofs, gardens and green, energy-efficient building materials.
New green amenities can push out low-income households through rising housing costs and can also displace long-time residents culturally and politically.
The term was first coined by Sieg and colleagues in 2004 and blends older ideas of gentrification and environmental justice.

contested_note: Sources say the exact definition of environmental gentrification remains a topic of debate.
distinct_from: Economics of green versus grey infrastructure

title: Barriers to green infrastructure

definition.text: The obstacles, above all a lack of funding, that slow the building of green infrastructure.

facts.text: Because green projects produce many benefits, they can compete for many different funding sources.
Some government tax incentive programs can be used to attract finance to green infrastructure projects.
In fragile states, weak governance and limited institutional capacity can stop countries benefiting from green infrastructure investment.

distinct_from: Economics of green versus grey infrastructure

title: Green infrastructure planning

definition.text: A planning approach that maps what the natural environment does and then protects key natural areas through regulation or planning policy.

facts.text: Where natural life-support functions are missing, plans may add them through landscaping or engineering.
In the UK it now appears in national, regional and local planning documents.
US programs run by the EPA aim to improve water quality by managing stormwater runoff more widely and easing the load on sewers.

distinct_from: Economics of green versus grey infrastructure

definition.text: A set of water management practices, also called SuDS, that make modern drainage work with natural water processes as part of a wider green infrastructure strategy.

facts.text: SuDS aim to reduce the harm development does to the natural water cycle, especially surface runoff and water pollution.
When vegetation is replaced by concrete, asphalt and roofs, land loses its ability to absorb rain, which then overloads drains and causes floods.
SuDS often bypass traditional drains and return rainwater to natural water bodies as soon as possible.
Typical components include bioswales, permeable paving, artificial wetlands, retention basins, green roofs, rain gardens and downspout disconnection.
Plants and soil remove stormwater pollutants by adsorption, filtration and plant uptake.
In urban areas covered mostly by hard surfaces, more than half of the rain becomes runoff.
Planting a rain garden to handle drainage usually costs less than digging tunnels and laying pipes.
Drainage systems have been found in ancient cities more than 5,000 years old, but modern systems appeared only in 19th-century Western Europe, mainly to deal with sewage.

definition.text: An artificial pond, also called a wet pond, with plants around its edge and a permanent pool of water, used to manage stormwater.

facts.text: It is used to control runoff, protect against floods and erosion, and improve the quality of nearby water.
It differs from a detention basin or 'dry pond', which holds water only after a storm and then drains at a controlled rate.
It also differs from an infiltration basin, which sends stormwater down to groundwater through permeable soil.

definition.text: The removal of pollutants and sediment from stormwater runoff by a planted soil area.

facts.text: A bioretention cell aims to reduce peak runoff and remove pollutants.
A typical cell has a sand bed, layers of filter media and plants on top; stored water seeps into the soil below over several days.
The name refers to plants and bacteria in the media that hold, absorb, break down and cycle contaminants.
Filtration, adsorption, chemical change and biological breakdown are its main ways of treating pollutants.
Untreated nitrogen and phosphorus in runoff cause eutrophication downstream; well-designed media can sharply reduce both.
In laboratory tests, cells removed 94% of zinc, 88% of copper, 95% of lead and more than 95% of cadmium at typical stormwater levels.
Its capacity for heavy metals is limited, so the media must eventually be replaced where metal loads are high.
Soils with more than 25 percent clay, slopes over 20 percent or unstable ground may rule it out.

definition.text: A channel, usually planted or mulched, that gathers and carries stormwater runoff while removing debris and pollution.

facts.text: It is a drainage course with gently sloped sides of less than 6%.
It is designed to keep water in the swale as long as safely possible, since longer stays remove more pollutants.
Plants catch pollutants, which then enter the soil and are broken down by bacteria.
Bioswales can also recharge groundwater, reduce flooding and erosion and give pollinators habitat.
They suit streets and parking lots, where car pollution is washed off by the first rain.
There are four types: low grass, vegetated, low water use and wet bioswales.
Poor maintenance can lead to high repair costs, so inspection at least once a year is advised.
In 1996, 2330 lineal feet of bioswale were installed at Willamette River Park in Portland, and check dams cut suspended solids entering the river by 50%.

definition.text: The first runoff of a rainstorm, which washes off pollution that has built up on hard surfaces.

facts.text: Urban and suburban first-flush runoff is described as highly toxic.
Bioswales are built to handle the first flush, so they suit roads, parking lots and roofs.
Rainwater tanks may use a first-flush diverter to keep contaminants out of stored water.

definition.text: The methods, also called flood control, used to reduce or prevent the harm done by flood waters.

facts.text: Floods come from a mix of natural causes, such as extreme weather upstream, and human changes to water bodies and runoff.
Methods are structural, which physically hold back water, or non-structural, which do not.
More hard surfaces, or wildfires that remove vegetation, make flooding worse.
Natural seasonal floods also do good: they renew soil fertility, restore wetlands and support biodiversity.
The cost of protection rises with the number of people and amount of property protected.
The US FEMA estimates that every $1.00 spent on mitigation saves $4.00.
Wetlands help manage floods, especially on coasts, by holding excess water and shielding inland communities from storm surges.

definition.text: Reducing flood effects with physical works such as reservoirs, levees, dredging and diversion channels.

facts.text: Some methods are ancient: planting vegetation to hold water, terracing hillsides and digging floodways to divert water.
Many dams keep reservoir levels low before the rainy or melt season to leave room for floodwater.
Levees, bunds, reservoirs and weirs keep rivers from bursting their banks.
Coastal flooding is met with sea walls, beach nourishment and barrier islands.
Excess floodwater can be diverted onto land that absorbs it, recharging groundwater and easing later droughts.

definition.text: Ways of reducing flood risk that do not physically hold back water, such as zoning, mapping, modelling and planning.

facts.text: Land zoning rules can limit how much is built on floodplains and other flood-prone areas.
Stakeholder engagement helps the public and officials agree on flood policy, including emergency and land-use planning.
Property owners can flood-proof homes by blocking doors and vents, waterproofing and sandbagging; such private measures are increasingly important.
Buildings can be designed for resilience, for example by raising homes on stilts, so a city recovers quickly after a flood.

title: Flood peak attenuation
article: Flood management#Flood levels: blunting the peak

definition.text: Slowing runoff so that a flood's short, steep peak is spread out over time and lowered.

facts.text: Flood water levels tend to rise and fall very abruptly.
Marshes, river meanders, vegetation, porous materials and a river spreading over its floodplain all slow parts of the flow and blunt the spike.

definition.text: Removing buildings from flood-prone areas and leaving the land as parks or wilderness.

facts.text: Floodplain buyout programs have run in New Jersey, Charlotte in North Carolina, and Missouri.

definition.text: A floodgate built to stop a storm surge or spring tide from flooding the area behind it.

facts.text: It is almost always part of a larger system of floodwalls, levees and natural features.
London's Thames Barrier has operated since 1982 to guard against surges like the North Sea flood of 1953.
Such barriers were introduced after the North Sea Flood of 1953.
Storm surge warnings help decide when to close the floodgates.

definition.text: Drawing maps of where floods may reach, so policy makers can make informed decisions about flood hazards.

facts.text: Producing flood risk maps is described as the most effective way to reduce risk to people and property, and most countries have them.
Flood modelling simulates flood hazards and how their drivers interact, and their effects on people and the environment.
In Bangladesh, where nearly 80% of people live on low floodplains, hazard maps pick out areas prone to repeated or severe floods.

definition.text: A shallow planted hollow, also called a bioretention facility, that helps rain runoff soak back into the soil.

facts.text: Rain gardens cut the speed, amount and pollution of runoff from roofs, driveways, parking lots and compacted lawns.
Plants and soil hold stormwater and filter pollutants carried by urban runoff.
Central urban areas can be 90 to 100 percent hard surfaces, against 5 to 10 percent in suburbs.
A typical soil mix is 60% sand, 20% compost and 20% topsoil.
Native plants are usually chosen because they tolerate local conditions, root deeply and add habitat.
Residential rain gardens began in 1990 in Prince George's County, Maryland, replacing a conventional stormwater pond, and proved highly cost-effective.
Water ponding for more than 48 hours may signal clogging, one of the most common problems.
A study rain garden in Xi'an held most of 28 large storms over four years; only 5 made it overflow.

definition.text: A planning and engineering approach, called WSUD, that builds the whole urban water cycle (stormwater, groundwater, wastewater and supply) into city design to limit environmental harm and improve amenity.

facts.text: WSUD is the term used in Australia and the Middle East; it resembles low-impact development in the United States and sustainable drainage systems in the United Kingdom.
It treats urban stormwater as a resource rather than a nuisance, a shift from conventional drainage that sent runoff quickly to streams.
Its principles include protecting urban creeks and wetlands, improving the quality of water leaving cities and maximizing reuse of stormwater, recycled water and greywater.
Common practices include bioretention systems, infiltration trenches, porous paving, sedimentation basins, constructed wetlands, swales and rainwater tanks.
The framework came out of Australia in the 1990s.
In Victoria, new residential developments must leave at least 20 percent of each site free of impervious surfaces.
Regulatory barriers and fragmented institutions across state and local government are major obstacles to its adoption.

title: Infiltration trench
article: Water-sensitive urban design#Infiltration trenches and systems

definition.text: A shallow trench filled with gravel or rock that holds stormwater underground and lets it seep slowly into the soil and groundwater.

facts.text: It is not mainly a treatment measure, but it can hold back some pollutants and sediment.
Sand filters work on the same principle and suit runoff from car parks and dense built-up areas.

definition.text: A basin that holds stormwater briefly and slows it so coarse and medium sediments settle out.

facts.text: It is often the first element of a treatment train, protecting later elements from being smothered by sediment.
Constructed wetlands often use a sedimentation basin as their inlet zone.

title: Floodplain restoration

definition.text: Returning all or part of a river's floodplain to its condition before levees were built and wetlands drained.

facts.text: Its goals include fewer floods, habitat for aquatic species, better water quality and more groundwater recharge.
Methods focus on reconnecting rivers to floodplains: setting back levees, removing dams or weirs, and restoring drained wetlands.
It is a nature-based solution that lowers flood risk by boosting the ecosystem's ability to slow and hold water.
Vegetation can cut wave energy during floods by about 70% in salt marshes and 65% in mangroves.
It works best for frequent, low to moderate floods and has limited benefit for extreme floods on its own.
Whether restoration increases coastal wetlands' carbon sequestration is debated, though their role in reducing flood risk is well supported.
Projects can stall when immediate flood defence and current land uses are valued above ecological benefits.
At Nijmegen, moving a dike 350 metres inland and digging a side channel lowered peak water levels by about 35 cm.

contested_note: Coastal wetlands are accepted as large carbon sinks, but whether restoration raises their sequestration rates is debated.

definition.text: Work to improve the environmental health of a river or stream, for biodiversity, recreation, flood management or landscape.

facts.text: Approaches split into form-based restoration, which physically alters the stream, and process-based restoration, which restores natural water and sediment processes.
It differs from river engineering, which alters water bodies for navigation, flood control or water supply without an ecological aim.
Activities range from fixing a culvert or removing a weir that blocks fish, to stabilizing banks, restoring riparian zones or adding constructed wetlands.
Projects usually begin by assessing climate, geology, hydrology, sediment transport, channel shape and flood records.
A US database built in the 2000s held over 35,000 stream restoration projects.
Its effectiveness remains poorly measured because of thin data, too little monitoring and differing yardsticks.
It is entering law, for example through the European water framework's commitment to restore surface waters.

title: Form-based stream restoration

definition.text: Restoration that changes a stream channel's physical shape to improve its condition.

facts.text: Tools include deflectors, cross-vanes, weirs and step-pools, engineered log jams, bank stabilization and channel reconfiguration.
It gives immediate change but can fail when degradation comes from a wider area.
Critics say it works at too small a scale and aims for what people think a stream should look like, not its geomorphic setting.

contested_note: Scientists criticize form-based restoration as working at too small a scale and imposing a socially preferred stream shape.

definition.text: Restoration that rebuilds the water and sediment processes that shape a stream, rather than its form.

facts.text: It has grown in popularity since the mid-1990s as a more ecosystem-centred approach.
It restores connections between stream and floodplain and along the stream, often by removing levees, dams or grade controls.
It aims to make the system as resilient as possible and need little maintenance, though benefits can take time to appear.

title: Natural Channel Design

definition.text: A US method from the 1990s that classifies a stream by its shape, slope and bed and then redesigns the channel to a target form.

facts.text: Its design phase has 8 phases and 40 steps.
Fluvial geomorphologists call it a 'cookbook' approach that untrained practitioners misuse, leading to failures.
Its focus on channel stability can limit a stream's ability to adapt.

contested_note: Fluvial geomorphologists criticize the method as a cookbook approach that can cause project failures.

title: Stream corridor (freedom space)
article: Stream restoration#Implementing a minimum stream corridor width

definition.text: A band of land, set by a stream's hydrology and geomorphology, within which the stream is left free to move with minimal intervention.

facts.text: The idea goes by many names: river corridor in the US, room for the river in the Netherlands, freedom space in France, making space for water in the UK.
A cost-benefit analysis found it could pay off long term through lower maintenance costs, less erosion and flood damage, and ecological services.

definition.text: Placing large wood in a stream to recreate the natural log jams that channelization and beaver removal took away.

facts.text: Log jams add riffles, pools and temperature variation to the flow.

definition.text: Stabilizing stream banks with live plants rather than only with hard structures such as riprap and gabions.

facts.text: Roots from sprouting live branches anchor the soil and prevent erosion.
This makes bioengineered structures more natural and adaptable than hard engineering.
Some bank erosion is generally seen as good for the diversity of aquatic and riparian habitats.

definition.text: A dam built by beavers, creating a pond that protects them from predators and stores food for winter.

facts.text: By reshaping their surroundings, beavers act as a keystone species and ecosystem engineers.
In their native range, beaver dams reduce downstream flooding, clean water, maintain wetlands and act as firebreaks.
The dam stores floodwater and releases it gradually, lowering the flood wave and sustaining flow in dry spells.
Bacteria in the debris behind dams turn nitrates into nitrogen gas and break down some pesticides.
Beaver ponds trapped 5.7 times more young wood frogs than nearby free-flowing streams in an Alberta study.
Dams typically run from a few metres to about 100 metres long; the largest known is 775 metres.
They can flood farmland, roads and railways, and introduced beavers in Tierra del Fuego are considered a plague.
Abandoned dams leave wetlands that become meadows and then forest, slowly building up valley bottomland.

definition.text: A human-built structure that imitates a beaver dam, to gain its benefits or to attract beavers to settle.

facts.text: Builders may drive wooden posts into the stream bed to hold branches that would otherwise wash away.
Even if beavers never take over, analogs provide many of the benefits of natural dams, such as water retention and wetland ponds.

definition.text: A North American land planning and engineering approach, called LID, that manages stormwater runoff as part of green infrastructure.

facts.text: It uses small engineered controls to copy a site's natural water regime by infiltrating, filtering, storing, evaporating and holding runoff near its source.
Similar terms include SuDS in the UK and water-sensitive urban design in Australia.
It began in Prince George's County, Maryland in 1990, because conventional detention ponds were not cost-effective and missed water quality goals.
Its five principles: conserve natural areas, minimize hydrological impact, keep runoff rate and duration, scatter small controls across the site, and prevent pollution.
Typical practices include rain gardens, pervious concrete, grassed swales and rainwater harvesting.
Research found LID rain gardens can hold up to 90% of water after a major storm and release it over up to two weeks.
It can remove the need for stormwater ponds on expensive land, letting developers build more homes on the same plot.
In some municipalities it is a cost-effective way to reduce combined sewer overflows.

definition.text: A nature-based urban planning model from China that uses green infrastructure, not just drains, to manage urban water and floods.

facts.text: The name reflects how green landscapes store, slow and soak up surface water like a sponge.
Its philosophy is to retain water at the source, slow its flow, clean it naturally and adapt where it collects, the reverse of grey infrastructure's pipes, reservoirs and walls.
Hard urban surfaces can raise surface flow from 10% to 60% and cut infiltration to nearly zero.
Proposed by landscape architect Kongjian Yu, it became national Chinese policy in 2014 after the 2012 Beijing flood killed 79 people.
Pilots began in 16 districts in 2015, growing to 87 cities by 2017.
Guidelines aim for cities to collect and use 70 percent of rainwater, on 20 percent of urban area by 2020 and 80 percent by 2030.
Studies show it reduces runoff and improves water quality, but monitoring data are scarce and 19 of 30 pilot cities have flooded since.

definition.text: Demolishing a dam to return natural water flow to a river.

facts.text: The case for removal weighs dams' benefits, such as hydropower, flood control, irrigation and navigation, against their harms.
Dams can reduce primary productivity, biodiversity and native species, and ageing brings weakness, sediment build-up and high maintenance costs.
About 900 US dams were removed between 1990 and 2015, and by 2015 the rate was 50 to 60 a year.
Many removals aim to restore river habitat and native fish, as in the Elwha Ecosystem Restoration.
Releasing trapped sediment can rebuild habitat downstream, but toxic sediment can do harm, as when PCBs were released after a Hudson River dam was removed.
Removal is always costly, and the cost is usually shared between the owner and government.
The European Commission counts at least 150 000 barriers in European rivers that no longer serve a purpose.
The EU Biodiversity Strategy aims to restore free flow to 25,000 kilometres of river by 2030.

definition.text: The four common ways of removing a dam, chosen mainly by how the sediment behind it is handled.

facts.text: Notch and release drains the reservoir slowly through cut notches so the ecosystem can adjust; it can take over a year.
Rapid release is quickest and cheapest but can cause severe flooding and erosion downstream.
Dig and dewater, usually the most expensive, removes dried sediment for safe disposal, needed when it contains toxins.
Retained sediment leaves the sediment in place and reroutes the river around the site.

title: Alternatives to dam removal

definition.text: Ways of reducing a dam's harm without removing it, such as better equipment, environmental flows and fish ladders.

facts.text: Fewer than 1% of US dams are being considered for removal.
Varying the water released by season mimics natural flow changes.
The effectiveness of fish ladders is debated, though some fish pass rather than none.
Plans for decommissioning and river restoration should be drawn up well before a dam reaches its design life.

contested_note: Sources debate how effective fish ladders are at letting fish reach spawning grounds.

title: Flood pulse concept

definition.text: The idea that a river's regular cycle of flooding and drying controls the exchange of water, nutrients and organisms between the channel and its floodplain.

facts.text: It treats the annual flood pulse as the most biologically productive feature of a river ecosystem, unlike older theories that saw floods as catastrophes.
The flood pulse maintains species and genetic diversity on the floodplain and brings in oxygen.
Dams, channelization, levees and other human changes disrupt the pulse and can devastate riparian ecosystems.
It was developed by W. J. Junk in 1989 and is one of three main models of large rivers, with the river continuum and serial discontinuity concepts.

contested_note: Many theorists criticize its assumptions and prefer the river continuum concept, while its authors argue that concept does not fit large rivers.

definition.text: Paving made of porous material, or of solid blocks with gaps, that lets stormwater pass through into the ground below.

facts.text: Materials include pervious concrete, porous asphalt, paving stones and interlocking pavers.
It reduces runoff and traps suspended solids, filtering pollutants from stormwater.
It can reduce downstream flooding and bank erosion and keep base flows in rivers.
Where soil cannot absorb water, the pavement stores it and releases it slowly between storms.
Some estimates put it at about one third more expensive than conventional paving, though it can reduce the need for other stormwater facilities.
Without regular cleaning its pores clog and it starts to behave like an impervious surface.
It should not be used at pollution 'hot spots' such as fuelling stations, where it could contaminate groundwater.

definition.text: The families of porous paving materials, each with its own advantages for particular uses.

facts.text: Pervious concrete is widely available and carries frequent traffic.
Porous asphalt is laid like normal asphalt but leaves out fine aggregate, so open voids let water through.
Plastic grids holding gravel or turf make a fully porous surface popular with homeowners.
Permeable interlocking concrete pavers have open spaces between units and carry light and heavy traffic.

definition.text: Bringing back riparian plants either by planting them (active) or by removing the disturbance and letting them return (passive).

facts.text: Active planting may be fastest but can be too costly in resources.
Fencing out cattle can let riparian plants recover quickly and shift toward natural communities.
Passive recovery can be undermined when exotic species colonize first.

title: Room for the River

definition.text: A Dutch government plan, run from 2006 to 2015, that protects against floods by giving the country's rivers more space while improving landscape and environment.

facts.text: It followed the 1993 and 1995 floods, when over 200,000 people near the Rhine delta were evacuated.
Measures included moving dykes back, lowering floodplains, lowering groynes, deepening side channels, removing obstacles and building a flood bypass.
A basic package of forty projects had a budget of €2.2 billion.
Its Nijmegen project marked a policy shift from ever-higher dikes toward working with natural river dynamics.

notes: Single-country programme kept because it is the chapter's seed and the standard international example of making room for rivers; demote if the course limits country cases.

definition.text: Planning by water utilities and governments to protect drinking water sources from overuse and contamination.

facts.text: It involves identifying sources, assessing contamination threats, informing the public and acting to remove contamination.
It applies to lakes, rivers and groundwater.
Canada adopted it as part of a multi-barrier approach after drinking water in Walkerton, Ontario was contaminated with E. coli.
Researchers have begun bringing ecosystem service assessments into source water protection.

definition.text: Water that comes from precipitation, including heavy rain and melted hail and snow.

facts.text: It can soak into soil to become groundwater, pond on the surface, evaporate, or run off over the land.
In forests and other natural landscapes, soil and plants absorb much of it.
In cities, unmanaged stormwater causes two main problems: flooding and water pollution.
Hard surfaces let less rain soak in, and drains rush runoff into waterways, causing erosion and floods and leaving little to recharge groundwater.
Most runoff reaches streams, rivers and other water bodies without treatment.
Phosphorus carried in runoff feeds algae and toxic cyanobacteria blooms in lakes.
Stormwater is a major cause of urban flooding.

definition.text: Managing the quantity and quality of stormwater, using both engineered controls and everyday practices known as best management practices.

facts.text: Best management practices include structures such as retention ponds and procedures such as street sweeping.
Technical measures include source control of hazardous materials, retention basins and filters, protecting natural waterways, and nature-based solutions working alongside pipes.
Institutional measures include stormwater user fees or utilities, asset management, updated regulations and community education.
Conventional facilities let particles larger than 40 micron settle out and hold water back to reduce flooding downstream.
Stormwater infrastructure is a costly long-term investment that performs worse as climate, urbanization and rules change.
In the US, the EPA regulates stormwater under the Clean Water Act, but farm runoff counts as nonpoint source pollution and needs no permit.

definition.text: Flooding of land or property in a built-up area when rain or coastal storm surges overwhelm drainage systems such as storm sewers.

facts.text: It can happen whether or not a community lies on a floodplain or near water.
Anything that enlarges impermeable surfaces, such as soil sealing, raises flood risk.
Climate change is expected to make storm surges, heavy rain and river overflow more frequent and severe.
In 2020, floods caused an estimated 6,000 deaths and US$51.3B in damages worldwide.
Where homes have basements, it is the main cause of basement and sewer backups, and chronically wet houses are linked to respiratory illness.
Responses include grey infrastructure, green infrastructure, better drainage and changing land use toward more vegetated open space.

definition.text: The three kinds of urban flood planners distinguish: pluvial (from heavy rain), fluvial (from a river overflowing) and coastal (often from storm surges).

facts.text: Each type has different impacts and needs different mitigation.
Erratic rainfall is expected to make both pluvial and fluvial flooding more frequent and severe.
Coastal cities may be hit hardest by sea level rise and heavier rain.

definition.text: Conventional infrastructure such as dams, seawalls, pipes and channels, built of concrete or other impervious materials to control water.

facts.text: It can prevent flood damage and be economically valuable, but models suggest it may grow less effective as climate change intensifies floods.
Grey approaches centralize water in big reservoirs, speed it through pipes and fight it with higher walls, the opposite of sponge city design.
Overuse of grey infrastructure can cause water shortages, pollution and loss of water ecosystem services.

definition.text: The financial costs urban floods impose on property owners, businesses and cities.

facts.text: US experts estimate wet basements can lower property values by 10%-25%.
FEMA says almost 40% of small businesses never reopen after a flooding disaster.
Urban flooding is estimated to cost £270 million a year in England and Wales.
In the UK, expected annual surface water damages may rise by £60–200 million under 2–4°C warming.

definition.text: Managing a city's freshwater, wastewater and stormwater together as parts of one river-basin plan.

facts.text: It is seen as a way to achieve the goals of water-sensitive urban design.
Managing the urban water cycle as a whole aims to use resources more efficiently, with economic, social and environmental gains.
Integrated stormwater management can improve runoff quality, cut flood risk and add to drinking water supply.
